\begin{abstract}
Medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmarks score whether an answer is right, not whether the model
looked at the image to produce it. A recent chest X-ray study found medical vision-language models (VLMs) to be
\emph{consistent but dangerous}: stable under rephrasing, yet unchanged when the image is removed. We test this
beyond chest X-rays, auditing MedGemma-4B against its architecture-matched, non-medical twin Gemma-3-4B on
3,365 questions over 907 CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology images (SLAKE, VQA-RAD, PathVQA). Each question is asked
with its image, without it, with a different image of the same modality, and in screened paraphrases, under a
pre-registered analysis. MedGemma is far more accurate (SLAKE yes/no 86.5\% \vs 68.7\%) and changes its answer
when the image changes. Yet when the image is \emph{missing} it keeps answering where Gemma-3 asks for the image,
and its blind answers beat the answer-frequency prior. Under the reference taxonomy this makes 13.7 points more
of its answers \dang{}\ci{10.0}{17.5}, but the excess consists entirely of \emph{correct} answers: stable,
image-independent and \emph{wrong} answers are equally common in both models (11.3\% \vs 11.7\%). Because
MedGemma errs less often, more of its remaining errors (44\% \vs 31\%) are of this kind, which consistency and
reliance checks cannot catch; image reliance does not flag wrong answers either (AUROC 0.51). We also show that
the \dang{} share rests on a large chance floor for yes/no questions and depends on how reliance is probed, and
we propose corrections.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not doing visual question
answering, however accurate it is. In general-domain VQA this concern produced balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still mostly evaluated by accuracy,
where it matters more: a correct answer reached from language priors will be wrong on exactly the patients
whose images are unusual.

Accuracy cannot separate \emph{seeing} from \emph{guessing well}, and consistency under rephrasing cannot
either: a model that ignores the image is often \emph{more} consistent, because nothing visual perturbs it.
Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore crossed the two per sample.
\emph{Consistent} means the answer is stable under paraphrase; \emph{image-reliant} means it changes when the
image is removed. This gives four quadrants: \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent but unchanged without the image) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays they found that
fine-tuning lowers paraphrase flip rates but moves most samples into \dang{}.

That study covered one modality, yes/no questions and one reliance probe. We ask four questions about a
small open medical VLM, MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma}, across CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology:
\textbf{Q1}~Does it answer better than chance \emph{without} the image? \textbf{Q2}~How large is the \dang{}
share per modality, and does it depend on how reliance is probed? \textbf{Q3}~Does image reliance flag wrong
answers better than the model's own confidence? \textbf{Q4}~What does medical post-training change? For Q4 we
compare against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, which has the same architecture and no medical
post-training. \Cref{fig:teaser} previews the answers on two real questions.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item A pre-registered, cross-modality audit of image reliance (3,365 questions, 18,896 model calls per model)
with an architecture-matched control, two reliance probes, image-clustered inference, and registered
robustness probes that address the main alternative explanations.
\item The consistent-but-dangerous pattern, separated into its parts: medical post-training adds answers that
are stable and image-independent \emph{and correct}; it does not add such answers that are wrong, but it makes
a larger share of the remaining errors undetectable by consistency or reliance checks.
\item Three properties of the quadrant taxonomy that change its interpretation: the \dang{} share has a large
chance floor on yes/no questions (we correct it with Cohen's $\kappa$); it depends on the reliance probe
($\kappa\le0.23$ between probes), and wrong-image probes are confounded by answer-preserving swaps; and
\dang{} answers are mostly correct, so the share must be split by correctness before it says anything about
risk.
\item An open, deterministic pipeline, including a paraphrase set screened pair by pair for semantic
equivalence and a finding that bf16 batching perturbs log-probabilities by up to 1~nat.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors in VQA.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors. Text-only baselines are
the medical analogue we build on.

\paragraph{Medical VQA reliability.} HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} tests whether models localize before
answering, and MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval} benchmarks hallucination and mitigation methods across
medical VLMs. Chen \etal~\cite{chen2026grounding} find that cropping to the ground-truth region hurts
closed-ended accuracy for MedGemma-4B and others.

\paragraph{Consistency and reliance.} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates of
3--37\% across nine medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates do not imply visual
grounding. The quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} combines both views; we extend it to other
modalities, open-ended answers, a second probe and a continuous score, and we examine its statistical
properties.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest is evaluated by
AUROC and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use it for Q3.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 questions from test and validation, the
only dataset with modality labels; validation is added so each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions, from the
original release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600
yes/no and 200 open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). A question is yes/no if its gold answer is
\emph{yes} or \emph{no}, as in the closed-ended splits of these benchmarks. The \textbf{primary analysis set}
is the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670 images. Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed
in committed manifests (SHA-1 seeded), so every run sees identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-style
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data; its model card lists
SLAKE (split unstated) but not VQA-RAD or PathVQA among training sources. It runs unquantized in bf16 on one
16\,GB GPU, which matters because quantization would perturb the very probabilities we audit.
\textbf{Gemma-3-4B} (\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) shares its architecture and size without the medical
training. The two differ in their whole post-training, not only in medical data, so we attribute differences
to MedGemma's post-training as a package. Both receive byte-identical prompts: a fixed system line, the
question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.'' or ``Answer with a single word or short phrase.''

\subsection{Probes}
Every question is posed under four conditions that differ only in the image or the wording:
\textbf{orig} (its image); \textbf{noimg} (image tokens omitted, otherwise identical text; the text-only
baseline of~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}); \textbf{shuf} (a different image from the same dataset and
modality, chosen by a hash of the question ID); and \textbf{para$_k$} (screened paraphrases, original image;
\cref{sec:para}). Removing image tokens is out-of-distribution input; a mismatched image is not, which is why
we use both. Three further probes, registered after the main run, are described in \cref{sec:probes}.

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} come from one forward pass:
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$ over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the raw first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is logged as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} use greedy decoding and token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with an opposite-term
guard (left/right, upper/lower, \etc never match). \textbf{Consistent}: the answer on the first two valid
paraphrases equals the \emph{orig} answer (fixed $K=2$ for every question). \textbf{Reliant} under a probe:
the probe answer differs from \emph{orig}. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from (consistent, reliant) under
either probe. \textbf{Image PMI} of an answer $\hat y$ is $\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat y\mid\varnothing,q)$:
how much the image raised the probability of the answer the model gave. \textbf{Abstention} without the image:
$m<0.5$, \ie most first-token mass is on neither \emph{yes} nor \emph{no}. \textbf{Chance correction}: Cohen's
$\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and probe answers; the \emph{chance floor} of the \dang{}
share is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$, where $p_e$ is the agreement expected from the two answer
distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates come
from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy; lexical, syntactic, formal, concise and question-frame
styles) and from two deterministic templates that copy every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X
present?'', ``does A show B?''$\to$``Is B shown in A?''). A rule validator rejects changes to laterality,
negation and absence words, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer leakage, near-copies
and length. Two audit rounds (100 and 300 fresh items) accepted 81\% and 83\%, below the pre-specified 85\%,
so we tightened the rules, excluded a ``plain language'' style (18/28 accepted), and then
\textbf{judged every unique rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair}, 4,890 in total, against a written rubric
(\cref{app:rubric}). The judge was an LLM (Claude); see \cref{sec:limits}. 1,208 pairs were rejected, each
with a recorded reason (\eg \emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}, \emph{does A show
B$\to$is A associated with B}), and unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. 84\% of the primary-set
questions retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use those (1,012 questions).

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were frozen before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every
later change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are labeled as such. Several questions share an
image, so all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$) with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Primary endpoints: \textbf{P1a--c} blind accuracy minus the
majority-answer prior, per dataset; \textbf{P2} AUROC(image PMI) $-$ AUROC(confidence) for predicting
correctness; both Holm-adjusted together~\cite{holm1979}; and \textbf{P3} the paired difference in \dang{}
share, MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3. A finding is called robust only if its sign holds across a grid of F1 thresholds
(0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and ``strong'' flips.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
Both runs completed (18,896 calls per model). Our pipeline reproduces MedGemma's published SLAKE score
(token-F1 70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3 on the model card; Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs 40.2), and the yes/no format mass
with the image is $\ge0.997$ in every dataset.

\subsection{Q1: Blind accuracy above the prior}
Without the image, both models fall to the prior on SLAKE (\cref{tab:acc}). MedGemma stays above it on
PathVQA, \textbf{P1a $=+5.0$\ci{0.9}{8.8}, $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.042$}, and on VQA-RAD (+7.6\ci{0.4}{14.5},
$p_{\text{Holm}}=0.072$); SLAKE is $-3.1$\ci{$-7.8$}{1.8}. Gemma-3 is never above the prior (+1.3, $-3.1$,
+2.4; all CIs include 0). Among questions MedGemma answers in format without the image ($m\ge0.9$), the
margin grows to +11.9\ci{7.1}{16.6} on PathVQA and +15.7\ci{5.1}{25.3} on VQA-RAD (post hoc).
Memorization of the test set is an unlikely explanation: the margin appears on the two datasets the model
card does not list as training data and not on SLAKE, which it does.

\subsection{Q2: Quadrants, modality and probes}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.png}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test). Left: reliance probed by removing the image (the
reference definition). Right: by a wrong image of the same modality. Shares are raw; on yes/no questions they
include chance agreement (\cref{sec:chance}) and correct answers (\cref{sec:harm}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

\Cref{fig:quad} shows the composition. Under the image-removed probe MedGemma's \dang{} share is
50.6/46.8/56.5\% (PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD), against 43.2/28.1/31.0\% for Gemma-3. Under the wrong-image probe
the two models are similar (46.6/64.7/61.9 \vs 44.1/70.8/63.7). The probes agree poorly: $\kappa$ between
``reliant without the image'' and ``reliant with a wrong image'' is 0.23, $-0.11$ and 0.18 for MedGemma and
0.07, 0.03 and 0.07 for Gemma-3. A \dang{} share is therefore underspecified without its probe.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig2_modality.png}
\caption{\dang{} share by modality (SLAKE yes/no, test and validation pooled as pre-specified; 95\% CIs by
image). The modality ordering reverses between probes.}
\label{fig:mod}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Modality} (\cref{fig:mod}). With the image removed, MedGemma's \dang{} share is about 50\% for CT
(50.8\ci{46.6}{55.6}) and MRI (50.0\ci{42.6}{57.4}) and lower for X-ray (33.1\ci{24.8}{41.2}). With a wrong
image the order reverses and X-ray is the highest (75.4\%). The reversal has a mechanical cause. Where the
partner image carries the same question we can read its gold answer: \emph{all 23} chest X-ray partners had
the same correct answer (CT 58\%, MRI 60\%), so an unchanged answer there is correct, not blind. On the 35
swaps whose correct answer does change, MedGemma changes its answer 74\% of the time and Gemma-3 17\%; the
registered opposite-answer probe (\cref{sec:probes}) tests this at scale.

\subsection{Q3: Does image reliance flag wrong answers?}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.png}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as a warning signal. We rank
each yes/no answer by its image PMI and measure how well this separates correct from incorrect answers
(\cref{fig:sel}). It does not: AUROC \textbf{0.513}\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma and 0.532 for Gemma-3, at
chance, while the model's own confidence reaches 0.709 and 0.603 (better by 0.197\ci{0.145}{0.250} and
0.071\ci{0.026}{0.116}). The wrong-image variant is no better (0.524, 0.536). Whether a model leaned on the
image does not tell us whether it was right.

\subsection{Q4: What medical post-training changes}
\paragraph{Abstention.} The pre-registered format check ($m\ge0.9$) failed in exactly one condition, image
removed (MedGemma 37--67\% of yes/no questions below 0.9, Gemma-3 18--76\%; with the image $\ge99.8\%$).
Free generation explains it (\cref{fig:teaser}a): ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image
to determine if there is a spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3); ``\emph{I am unable to answer this question as I
do not have access to medical images}'' (MedGemma, elsewhere). This is behavior, not a bug, so we keep the
pre-registered forced-choice $P(\text{yes})$ and report abstention as an outcome (\cref{fig:abst}). Gemma-3
abstains on 14.0, 40.6 and 50.2\% of questions (PathVQA, SLAKE, VQA-RAD), MedGemma on 9.7, 26.2 and 27.1\%;
paired difference $-11.2$\ci{$-14.0$}{$-8.6$}~points.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.png}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model mostly does not answer yes/no when the image is removed
($m<0.5$; 95\% CIs by image).}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{P3.} MedGemma's \dang{} share is \textbf{13.7 points higher}\ci{10.0}{17.5} ($p<0.001$; 1,012
questions, 600 images), positive in every dataset (PathVQA +7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9},
VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}) and in every cell of the sensitivity grid. Removing questions on which either
model abstains reduces it to +8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3} (both $m\ge0.9$, $n=436$) or +12.6\ci{8.1}{17.0} (both
$m\ge0.5$). Under the wrong-image probe it is $-0.7$\ci{$-4.4$}{3.2} (\cref{fig:p3}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_p3.png}
\caption{The MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3 difference in \dang{} share under each probe and subset, and split by whether
the \dang{} answer is correct (paired; 95\% CIs by image).}
\label{fig:p3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{How much of \dang{} is chance?}
\label{sec:chance}
An answer counts as image-independent whenever the no-image answer \emph{equals} the with-image answer, which on
yes/no questions happens often by chance. On the P3 set, MedGemma's answers are unchanged without the image
58.6\% of the time against 49.1\% expected from its answer distributions alone (Gemma-3: 49.7\% \vs 45.7\%).
Combined with consistency, this gives a \textbf{chance floor of 41.5\% (MedGemma) and 35.8\% (Gemma-3)} against
observed \dang{} shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%: Gemma-3 is at its floor and MedGemma 9 points above it. About 6
of the 13.7 points of P3 are the difference in floors, partly because MedGemma is more consistent (84.5\% \vs
78.4\% of questions), a desirable property the quadrant metric counts against it. Corrected for chance, the
effect remains: $\kappa(\text{orig},\text{noimg})=0.186$\ci{0.126}{0.250} \vs 0.074\ci{0.022}{0.128},
$\Delta\kappa=+0.112$\ci{0.044}{0.180}, $p=0.002$.

\subsection{Is \dang{} dangerous?}
\label{sec:harm}
A \dang{} answer is stable and image-independent, but it may well be correct. Splitting by correctness (post
hoc; \cref{fig:p3}, bottom) shows that \textbf{the entire P3 gap consists of correct answers}: \dang{}-and-correct
is 39.2\% for MedGemma and 25.1\% for Gemma-3 (+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}), while \dang{}-and-wrong, the cell that
would mislead a user, is 11.3\% and 11.7\% ($-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0}). MedGemma makes 12.0 points fewer errors
overall, so a larger share of its remaining errors are \dang{}: \textbf{44\% \vs 31\%}
(+12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}). These are the errors that neither a consistency check nor an image-reliance check would
flag.

\subsection{Robustness probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Three alternative explanations were registered and tested after the main run, before running the probes (one
Holm-adjusted family; App.~\ref{app:dev}). \textbf{R1, black image instead of no image}: is ``answering
without the image'' only confusion from missing image tokens? \textbf{R2, ``unknown'' allowed}: is it only
compliance with ``Answer with only yes or no''? \textbf{R3, opposite-answer image}: for 367 SLAKE questions,
another image of the same modality on which the same question has the opposite correct answer; does the model
change its answer when it should? \pending{Probe results to be inserted after the run (H6--H8).}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{What medical post-training changes.} With an informative image present, MedGemma uses it: it is 18
points more accurate than Gemma-3 on SLAKE yes/no and changes its answer when the image's answer changes.
What its post-training adds is a willingness to answer \emph{without} the image, with answers that beat the
prior, agree with its image-based answers beyond chance, and are usually right. This reproduces the
\emph{consistent but dangerous} pattern reported for fine-tuned chest X-ray models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}
on CT, MRI, X-ray, radiology and pathology, but with a different reading: the extra \dang{} answers are mostly
correct answers from priors, not new failures. The risk is subtler. MedGemma's errors are fewer, but more of
them look exactly like its correct answers to every check we can run without labels: stable under
paraphrase, unchanged without the image, and confidently given. In deployment they would surface when an image
fails to load, is the wrong study, or is uninformative.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Report the \dang{} share with its chance floor or as
$\kappa$; on balanced yes/no data a model whose blind answers are pure noise is about 50\% ``not reliant''.
(2)~Split \dang{} by correctness; the share alone mixes useful priors with real failures. (3)~Use more than
one probe and report their agreement: removing the image measures willingness to answer blind, a wrong image
measures sensitivity to content, and the latter needs answer-changing swaps. (4)~Treat abstention without the
image as a desirable behavior, not a format failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
One audited model and one control are not a population of models, and the two differ in their whole
post-training, not only in medical data; more model pairs are needed before generalizing to ``medical
tuning''. SLAKE is in MedGemma's training data (split unstated). Abstention is inferred from first-token mass
and confirmed on a sample by free generation, not annotated per question. Paraphrase equivalence was judged by
an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by human raters}; this is the main limitation of the consistency measure,
and an LLM judge may share blind spots with the paraphraser. PathVQA questions are auto-generated and often
ungrammatical. The correctness split (\cref{sec:harm}) and the chance correction were added after seeing the
results. All 330 pilot questions used to tune the design are inside the evaluation set; excluding them leaves
every conclusion unchanged (P1a +6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}, P3 +12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}). Benchmark VQA is not clinical use,
and nothing here is a clinical claim.

\section{Implementation Details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} A Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line interface: \texttt{prepare}
(download, deterministic sampling, SHA-checked images), \texttt{paraphrase} (generation plus rule and
judgment validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in parts with checkpoint analysis),
\texttt{probes} (the registered robustness probes), \texttt{analyze}, \texttt{compare} and \texttt{posthoc}
(all tables and figures here). Configs layer base, profile, model and hardware settings. Each job is one
(question, condition) pair keyed by ID, so interrupted runs resume without recomputation, and every run records
its config, commit and library versions.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19, bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080
SUPER (16\,GB). A full run is 18,896 calls per model at 0.23\,s per call (about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak).
During pre-flight we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up
to 1.09 nats (median 0.17) even with identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most
0.008. An fp32 output head did not remove it, so the cause is inside the network. All runs therefore use
batch size 1, which costs about 1.5$\times$ throughput. A regression check reproduced the T4 pilot on the new
GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean $|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 95 unit tests and 7 real-model tests cover, among others, scoring edge cases, paraphrase
rules (including each failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resume, the
coverage of the clustered bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, chance agreement of
$\kappa$, and the construction of opposite-answer partners.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
Medical post-training makes a small VLM better at looking and more willing to answer without looking. The
second effect is mostly benign, because the blind answers it adds are usually right, but it hides the
remaining errors among answers that look trustworthy and do not depend on the image. Measuring this reliably
requires chance correction, a correctness split, and more than one reliance probe.

\appendix
\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if it asks exactly the same thing, so the correct answer cannot differ.
Allowed: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
fact turned into a possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be enlarged?'');
a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract, skull
fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modality (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or changed relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass
lateral to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy,
coronal$\to$transverse); two questions in one; malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364,
modal 106, added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus
template-pass rejections).
